author: LITUBO Applications
title_en: Poultry Processor Achieves Zero Bone Complaints [TEST]
excerpt_en: How a large poultry producer eliminated bone fragment complaints with LITUBO X-ray systems. [TEST DATA]
body_en:
Challenge

A European poultry processor was receiving customer complaints about bone fragments in boneless chicken fillets.

Solution

LITUBO LX-5000 X-ray inspection systems installed at the end-of-line with real-time rejection and automatic reporting.

Results

Zero bone fragment complaints in 18 months post-installation.
seo_description_en: Case study: zero bone complaints with LITUBO X-ray. [TEST DATA]

title_en: Can X-rays penetrate all packaging types? [TEST]
excerpt_en: FAQ about X-ray penetration through various packaging materials. [TEST DATA]
body_en: Yes. X-ray inspection is effective through metal cans, foil pouches, glass jars, plastic trays and cardboard boxes. The X-ray beam penetrates the packaging and the product; only dense foreign bodies are flagged.

title_en: How often should inspection systems be calibrated? [TEST]
excerpt_en: FAQ: recommended calibration intervals for LITUBO inspection systems. [TEST DATA]
body_en: LITUBO recommends daily performance verification using certified test pieces at the start of each production shift. Full calibration should be performed by a certified technician at least once per year, or after any major maintenance.

title_en: Why is metal detection harder with wet or conductive products? [TEST]
excerpt_en: FAQ: product effect on metal detector performance. [TEST DATA]
body_en: High-moisture and high-salt products conduct electricity and can mimic a metal signal. Modern metal detectors use multi-frequency technology to separate the product effect from genuine metal contamination, maintaining sensitivity without false rejects.

author: LITUBO Applications Team
title_en: Metal Detector Sensitivity: A Technical Guide [TEST]
excerpt_en: Understanding sensitivity parameters to match your metal detector to your product and packaging requirements. [TEST DATA]
body_en:
Sensitivity Factors

Metal detector sensitivity depends on aperture size, operating frequency, product effect, and environmental conditions.

  • Ferrous metals: easiest to detect
  • Non-ferrous metals: moderate sensitivity
  • Stainless steel: most challenging
seo_description_en: Technical parameters for metal detector sensitivity. [TEST DATA]

author: LITUBO Editorial
title_en: X-Ray Inspection: Food Safety 101 [TEST]
excerpt_en: A concise overview of how X-ray inspection protects food products from physical contaminants. [TEST DATA - DO NOT PUBLISH]
body_en:
Introduction

X-ray inspection systems detect dense foreign bodies such as metal, glass, stone and bone in packaged and bulk food products.

How It Works

A focused X-ray beam passes through the product. Dense objects absorb more radiation and appear as darker areas on the image, which are flagged by the system automatically.
seo_description_en: Learn the basics of X-ray food safety inspection. [TEST DATA]

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: What to prepare before requesting an inspection quotation
excerpt_en: A clear brief shortens the path from enquiry to a usable quotation. These are the details suppliers usually need.
body_en:
An inspection quotation is only as good as the information behind it. A short, specific brief gets you a more useful answer.

Useful details to include

  • Product type, pack format and pack size
  • Contaminants you need to detect
  • Line speed and packs per minute
  • Packaging material
  • Available space and installation constraints
  • Any weight or labelling requirements

What happens next

The supplier reviews the brief, may ask for samples, and confirms the configuration with you before quoting.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Fitting inspection equipment into an existing line
excerpt_en: Space, product flow and reject handling usually decide the layout more than the inspection technology itself.
body_en:
Most inspection projects are constrained by the line, not the detector. Planning the fit early avoids costly rework.

Check before ordering

  • Available length and width at the intended position
  • Conveyor height and transfer points
  • Where rejected product can go
  • Access for cleaning and test routines
  • Power, air and network connections

A practical approach

Measure the space first, then choose the technology and frame size that fits it.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Understanding inspection sensitivity and product effect
excerpt_en: Sensitivity is not a single number. It depends on the contaminant, the product and the packaging together.
body_en:
Suppliers often quote a sensitivity figure, but that figure is only meaningful for a defined product and contaminant. Change the product and the number changes.

The main variables

  • Contaminant material and size
  • Product density, moisture and salt content
  • Packaging material, especially foil and metalised film
  • Line speed

What to ask for

Ask for the test conditions behind any sensitivity claim, and ask for a test on your own product.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: How do I get a quotation?
body_en: Send your product type, pack format, contaminants to detect, line speed, packaging material and any space constraints. Our team reviews the brief and confirms the configuration before quoting.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Preparing a product sample for inspection testing
excerpt_en: Inspection performance depends on your real product and packaging. A good sample set makes the test meaningful.
body_en:
Before a system is specified, the supplier should test your actual product. The quality of that test depends on the sample you send.

What to include

  • Product in its final packaging
  • A range of typical and worst-case packs
  • Representative contaminant samples, if available
  • Your expected line speed and pack rate

Why it matters

A test on a different product or pack size can give a misleading result. Real samples keep the specification honest.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Can I get a manual for my machine?
body_en: Manuals are supplied with the machine. If you need a replacement copy, send the model and serial number through the support request form.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Do you provide operator training?
body_en: Yes. Operator and maintenance training can be arranged as part of a project or as a separate service visit. Scope and schedule are confirmed with your team.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: How do I request spare parts?
body_en: Send the machine model and serial number, plus the part description or a photo, through the spare-parts request form. We will confirm the correct part for your unit.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Can you inspect frozen products?
body_en: Yes. Frozen products can be inspected, but ice crystals and product density affect both X-ray and metal detection performance. Testing with frozen samples is recommended.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Which industries do you serve?
body_en: LITUBO focuses on food and packaging production, including bakery, meat and seafood, frozen food, bottled and canned products, powders and granules, and pharmaceutical or daily-chemical packs.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Can a checkweigher reject out-of-weight packs?
body_en: Yes. A checkweigher compares each pack against the target range and can activate a pusher, air blast, drop flap or other reject device for non-conforming packs.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: What accuracy can a checkweigher achieve?
body_en: Accuracy depends on the pack weight relative to the weigh cell, belt speed, pack stability and vibration at the installation point. A typical reference figure is stated per model, but the actual result is confirmed on your line.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Conveyors and reject systems for inspection lines
excerpt_en: The reject system is where inspection becomes action: a pusher, air blast, drop flap or retracting belt removes the failed pack.
body_en:
An inspection system is only as useful as its reject. The reject type depends on product shape, speed and how the failed pack must be handled.

Common reject types

  • Pusher — simple and positive for rigid packs
  • Air blast — fast, for light packs
  • Drop flap — for bulk or loose product
  • Retracting belt — gentle, for fragile packs

Conveyor considerations

Belt material, guide rails and transfer points all affect pack stability, which in turn affects inspection reliability.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Why does a wet product affect metal detection?
body_en: Wet, salty or hot products can disturb the detector field themselves. This is called product effect. Modern detectors compensate with phase discrimination, but the compensation has limits, which is why product testing matters.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: What metals can a metal detector find?
body_en: A standard metal detector finds ferrous, non-ferrous and stainless-steel contamination. Sensitivity depends on the aperture size, the product and the line speed.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Do I need to send product samples?
body_en: We recommend it. A test with your real product in its final packaging gives a meaningful performance figure. A test on a different product or pack size can mislead.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Can X-ray inspect products in aluminium trays or foil?
body_en: Yes. Unlike metal detection, X-ray inspection is not blocked by aluminium trays, foil or metalised film. The packaging does affect the image, so the system settings are confirmed against your actual pack.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: What can X-ray inspection detect?
body_en: X-ray inspection reacts to density differences. It can detect metal, stone, glass, bone, dense plastics and some other foreign objects inside packaged products. The achievable sensitivity depends on the product, the packaging and the contaminant, so it is always confirmed by testing your real product.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Combining inspection technologies on your line
excerpt_en: Combination systems put X-ray, metal detection and checkweighing in one frame with a single reject, saving floor space and operator time.
body_en:
A combination system integrates more than one inspection technology on a single conveyor. Depending on the configuration, a reject station removes a pack that fails a check.

Typical combinations

  • Metal detection + checkweighing
  • X-ray + checkweighing
  • X-ray + metal detection + checkweighing

What to plan for

  • Available line length and the reject position
  • How each technology’s test routine is scheduled
  • Data and records from all technologies in one place

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: Checkweighing basics: keeping fill weights compliant
excerpt_en: A checkweigher compares each pack against a target weight and rejects packs outside the allowed range. It is a compliance tool, not just a quality tool.
body_en:
A dynamic checkweigher weighs each pack as it moves across the belt. Packs outside the target range are rejected or flagged.

What determines accuracy

  • Belt speed and pack stability
  • Pack weight relative to the weigh cell capacity
  • Vibration and air movement at the installation point
  • Product build-up on the belt

Why it matters

Under-filling breaches weight regulations; over-filling gives away product. A checkweigher gives you a record of both.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: How metal detection works and when to use it
excerpt_en: Metal detectors use a balanced coil system: a clean product passes without a signal, and a metal contaminant disturbs the field.
body_en:
A metal detector generates an electromagnetic field through its aperture. When a conductive or magnetic particle passes, the field changes and the system registers a detection.

The product effect

Wet, salty or hot products can themselves disturb the field. Modern detectors compensate for this with phase discrimination, but the compensation has limits.

Practical checks

  • Test with the actual contaminant types you care about
  • Test at the real line speed and loading
  • Re-test after product or packaging changes

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: X-ray or metal detection: which system fits your product?
excerpt_en: The choice between X-ray and metal detection usually comes down to what you need to find, what the product is packed in, and how much space the line has.
body_en:
Metal detection reacts to metal contaminants. X-ray inspection reacts to density differences, so it may also find stone, glass, bone and some plastics; what is detectable depends on the product and the test.

When metal detection is a good fit

  • The main risk is ferrous, non-ferrous or stainless metal
  • The product is dry, homogeneous and low in salt or moisture variation
  • You need a simple, compact installation

When X-ray is a good fit

  • You need to find non-metal contaminants
  • The product is in aluminium trays, foil or metalised film
  • You also want fill-level or structural checks

Many lines use both technologies. Combination systems run them on one frame with a shared reject.

author: LITUBO Team
title_en: How X-ray inspection works in food production
excerpt_en: A plain-language overview of how an X-ray inspection system finds dense contaminants inside packaged products, and what that means for line operators.
body_en:
An X-ray inspection system passes a low-dose beam through the product and measures how much of it is absorbed. Dense materials — metal, stone, glass, some plastics and bone — absorb more than food or packaging, so they appear as darker regions in the image.

What the system sees

The detector converts the transmission into a grayscale image. The system then applies thresholds and shape rules to decide whether a region is a contaminant or normal product structure.

What affects performance

  • Product density and thickness
  • Packaging material and thickness
  • Contaminant material, size and orientation
  • Line speed and belt loading

Because these factors interact, inspection performance is always confirmed against your real product and packaging, not assumed from a catalogue.
